channel.title: FishCare AI — Aquarium Care Guides
channel.description: New aquarium fish care guides, species care sheets and fish health troubleshooting from FishCare AI.

item.title: Oscar White Spots? Ich or Hole-in-the-Head — How to Tell
item.description: Salt-grain white spots all over an oscar are usually ich; pale pits on the head are hole-in-the-head (HLLE). How to tell them apart and treat each one.

item.title: Neon Tetra Hiding? Usually Group Size, Light or a New Tank
item.description: Neon tetras hide when the group is too small, the tank is bright and bare, or they are new. How to check, and when hiding points to neon tetra disease.

item.title: Honey Gourami Hiding? Usually Shyness, Open Tanks or Bullies
item.description: Honey gouramis are shy and hide in open tanks or with boisterous fish. How to tell shyness from stress or illness, and how to get yours out in the open.

item.title: Guppy Hiding? Often Birth Is Close or Males Are Harassing
item.description: A hiding female guppy is often close to giving birth or escaping males. How to check, fix the male-to-female ratio, and spot illness in a hiding guppy.

item.title: Dwarf Gourami Losing Color? Stress First, but Rule Out DGIV
item.description: A fading dwarf gourami is usually stressed or not displaying, but dwarf gouramis often carry iridovirus (DGIV). How to tell the difference and what to do.

item.title: Koi Not Eating? Check the Water Temperature First
item.description: Koi eat less as ponds cool and barely at all in cold water. How to tell a normal seasonal slowdown from low oxygen, parasites or koi herpesvirus.

item.title: Guppy Breathing Fast? Test Ammonia and Oxygen First
item.description: A guppy breathing fast is usually reacting to ammonia, nitrite, low oxygen or heat. What to test first, when it is gill flukes, and how to fix it today.

item.title: Guppy Curled or Bent Body? Genetics, Water or Fish TB
item.description: A bent guppy is often born that way, but a sudden curl means test the water today. How to tell inherited curves from toxins and mycobacteriosis.

item.title: Flowerhorn Losing Color? Often Fading, Not Disease
item.description: A flowerhorn losing its black markings is usually a natural fader. How to tell fading from stress, boosted shop colour, diet and water problems.

item.title: Flowerhorn Cloudy Eye? Usually Injury or Water, Not Disease
item.description: A cloudy eye on a flowerhorn is most often an injury or poor water, not a disease. How to tell one eye from both, when it is infection, and what to do.

item.title: Flowerhorn Suddenly Aggressive? Often Breeding or Territory
item.description: A flowerhorn that turns aggressive is usually maturing, ready to breed or defending new territory. How to find the trigger and keep tank mates safe.

item.title: Ember Tetra Losing Color? Settling In, Stress or Diet
item.description: Pale ember tetras are usually young, female, new or stressed. How to bring back the orange-red with the right group, tank, diet and water.

item.title: Cardinal Tetra White Spots? Usually Ich — Start Treating Now
item.description: Salt-grain white spots on a cardinal tetra are almost always ich. How to confirm it, treat safely in soft water, and rule out velvet, cysts and columnaris.

item.title: Cardinal Tetra Losing Color? Usually Night Fade or Stress
item.description: Cardinal tetras fade every night and when stressed. How to tell normal pallor from bright-light, water or neon tetra disease problems, and what to fix.

item.title: Blood Parrot Swimming Sideways? Buoyancy, Food or Water
item.description: Blood parrots are prone to buoyancy problems from their hybrid body shape. How to tell a feeding issue from bad water or infection, and what to do today.

item.title: Blood Parrot Losing Color? Often Shop Color or Dye Fading
item.description: A blood parrot that fades after purchase is usually losing colour food or dye, not sick. How to read the colour change and when it signals a problem.

item.title: Black Neon Tetra Pale? Why the Black Stripe Fades
item.description: A black neon's dark band fades with stress, a pale bright tank and at night. How to tell normal fading from water problems or neon tetra disease.

item.title: Black Neon Tetra Hiding? Usually New, Alone or Outnumbered
item.description: Black neon tetras hide when newly moved, kept in too small a group or with bullies. How to tell normal shyness from water problems or early disease.

item.title: Betta Black Spots? Usually Marble Genes or Healing Pigment
item.description: Flat black patches on a betta are usually marble colour genes or pigment returning after injury. When it is ammonia, a tumour or true black spot disease.

item.title: Honey Gourami Bloated? Overfeeding, Eggs or Dropsy
item.description: A tiny honey gourami bloats easily on too much dry food, and ripe females swell with eggs. How to tell these from dropsy, worms or gourami iridovirus.

item.title: Giant Gourami Bloated? Diet, Eggs or Infection
item.description: A bloated giant gourami is usually overfed on rich food; mature females also fill with eggs. How to tell these from bacterial infection and ISKNV.

item.title: Common Pleco Torn Fins? Usually Injury — or Fin Rot
item.description: Torn fins on a common pleco usually come from tank mates, tight caves or nets. How to tell a clean injury from fin rot, and how to help fins regrow.

item.title: Common Pleco Not Eating? Often It Feeds at Night
item.description: Most plecos that seem to refuse food are eating after dark or losing food to tank mates. How to check the belly, what to feed, and when it is illness.

item.title: Common Pleco Losing Color? Often Normal — or Stress
item.description: Plecos lighten and darken with light, background and mood. How to tell a normal colour shift from stress, bad water or infection causing pale patches.

item.title: Common Pleco Hiding? Usually Normal — When to Worry
item.description: Common plecos hide by day because they are nocturnal. How to confirm yours is feeding at night, and the signs that hiding means stress or illness.

item.title: Bristlenose Pleco Torn Fins? Often Males Fighting
item.description: Torn fins on a bristlenose pleco usually mean males fighting over caves. How to tell fight damage from fin rot, and how many caves and males to keep.

item.title: Bristlenose Pleco Pale? Normal Colour Change or Stress
item.description: Bristlenose plecos lighten and darken to match their background, so brief paleness is normal. How to tell it from stress, bad water or disease.

item.title: Bristlenose Pleco Not Eating? Check for Night Grazing
item.description: Most bristlenose that seem not to eat are grazing at night, settling in, or a male guarding eggs. How to check droppings and belly, and when to worry.

item.title: Bristlenose Pleco Bloated? Eggs, Overfeeding or Dropsy
item.description: A round-bellied bristlenose is usually overfed or a female full of eggs. How to sex it, check the belly and tell diet bloat from dropsy or parasites.

item.title: Weather Loach Jumping? Pressure Changes, Warm Water & Lids
item.description: Weather loaches get restless and jump when air pressure changes, which is how they got their name. Why yours is jumping and how to stop it escaping.

item.title: Weather Loach Floating at the Top? Too Warm or Short of Air
item.description: Weather loaches gulp air, but one that hangs at the surface is usually too warm or short of oxygen. How to tell normal air breathing from real trouble.

item.title: Silver Arowana Not Eating? New-Tank Stress or Wrong Food
item.description: A new silver arowana often refuses food for days. How to tell settling-in stress and food refusal from cold water, poor water quality and illness.

item.title: Silver Arowana Jumping? It's Hunting Instinct — Lid It Now
item.description: Silver arowana leap from the water to catch insects in the wild, so jumping in a tank is instinct. Why it happens, what triggers it and how to stop injuries.

item.title: Oscar Fish Jumping? Startled by Lights, Feeding or Bad Water
item.description: Oscars jump when startled, often by lights switched on in a dark room, or when lunging for food. How to stop it and rescue an oscar on the floor.

item.title: Molly Jumping Out of Tank? Male Harassment or Low Oxygen
item.description: Female mollies flee relentless males; mollies gasping at the surface mean low oxygen. How to tell which, fix it today, and save a molly on the floor.

item.title: Guppy Jumping Out of Tank? Natural Leaps or Harassed Females
item.description: Guppies are proven jumpers, and females chased by males try hard to get away. How to tell that from bad water, and what to do for a guppy found on the floor.

item.title: Goldfish Jumping Out of Tank? Low Oxygen or Ammonia
item.description: A goldfish that jumps is usually escaping stale water: low oxygen or ammonia in a small, crowded tank. How to test, fix it today and rescue a fish on the floor.

item.title: Betta Fish Jumping? Open Tops, Strong Current or Bad Water
item.description: Bettas live at the surface and jump readily. Why yours leaps — open tank, strong filter, cold or dirty water — and how to rescue a betta found on the floor.

item.title: Betta Floating at the Top? Resting, Bloated or Sick
item.description: A betta at the surface is often just resting or breathing air. How to tell normal rest from overfeeding, swim bladder trouble and a fish that is dying.

item.title: Guppy Bloated? Pregnant, Overfed or Dropsy — How to Tell
item.description: A bloated female guppy is usually pregnant. How to check the gravid spot, and how to tell overfeeding, Camallanus worms and dropsy apart.

item.title: How to Get Rid of Algae in Fish Tank: 7 Steps That Work
item.description: How to get rid of algae in fish tank glass, gravel and plants in 7 steps: light, nutrients, water changes, scrubbing, flow, algae eaters and safe drops.

item.title: Filtration Canister Guide: Choosing a Tank Canister Filter
item.description: Filtration canister guide: how a tank canister filter works, the flow rate per gallon, what media to load, how often to clean it and what public aquariums use.

item.title: Black Beard Algae: How to Identify and Kill BBA
item.description: Black beard algae identified and treated: what causes BBA, how to kill it with hydrogen peroxide and siamese algae eaters, and how it differs from brown algae.

item.title: Siamese Algae Eaters: True SAE vs Chinese Algae Eater
item.description: Siamese algae eaters explained: how to tell a true SAE from the flying fox and chinese algae eater fish, what they eat, tank size and why they stop grazing.

item.title: Algae Eater Fish: Best Algae Eaters for Freshwater Tanks
item.description: Algae eater fish compared by tank size and algae type: otocinclus, siamese algae eater, bristlenose pleco, nerite snail and amano shrimp, plus the two to avoid.

item.title: Grouper Fish Water Parameters: Temperature, Salinity, pH
item.description: Grouper fish water parameters: 74–80°F, salinity 1.023–1.026, pH 8.1–8.4, nitrate under 30 ppm, and the skimmer and water changes a predator's bioload demands.

item.title: Types of Grouper Fish for the Aquarium: 12 Species Compared
item.description: Types of grouper fish for the aquarium: miniatus, panther, leopard, bluespotted, lyretail and blue-line hind compared by adult size, minimum tank, temperament.

item.title: Grouper Fish Tank Size: Minimum Gallons by Species
item.description: Grouper fish tank size by species: 75–100 gallons for dwarf hinds, 100–125 for miniatus, 180 for panther groupers, 180–300 for bluespotted and lyretail.

item.title: Grouper Fish Tank Mates: What Can Live With a Grouper
item.description: Grouper fish tank mates: the lionfish, tangs, angels, triggers and eels that work, the clownfish, gobies and shrimp that get eaten, and reef safety.

item.title: Grouper Fish Size and Lifespan: How Big and How Fast
item.description: Grouper fish size in the aquarium by species (8 inches for dwarf hinds to 30 for lyretail), growth of 6–10 inches in year one, and a lifespan of 10–20 years.
